extracted.intended_audience: writers, poets, painters, and artists seeking to create distinctively American literature or landscape art (especially those depicting the Western United States)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating poetry, prose, and visual art grounded in the American West: how to observe, select subjects, and adapt forms and diction to produce an authentically American literature and art. Emphasizes direct experience of prairies, mountains, rivers, and frontier life and how those feed aesthetic creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctively American literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature worthy of the United States should be 'entirely western, fresh and limitless—altogether our own, without a trace or taste of Europe's soil, reminiscence, technical letter or spirit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Prairies, the Plains, the Mississippi and Missouri rivers, and the character and life of the West as the concrete background and imaginative source for work that fuses national identity and local reality; avoid reliance on imported British or classical models as the normative standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground art in direct experience of Western landscapes
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists and writers should make 'feeding visits' to the West—sketching and studying on-site—because these regions supply unique material not found in Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman insists that poets, painters, colorists, and other artists must personally study the Rockies, prairies, and Mississippi valley to internalize their shapes, lights, and materials; such direct observation can render previous studio work 'muddy, raw and artificial' in comparison and may prompt discarding old approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study and represent unique regional natural features (e.g., mountain streams)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Nothing like the water of pastoral plains... The shapes that element takes in the shows of the globe cannot be fully understood by an artist until he has studied these unique rivulets.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to the specific behavior and visual forms of local natural elements (mountain streams, snow-patches, cañons) and render them faithfully; avoid generic or pastoralized treatments borrowed from other regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture novel aerial effects and atmospheric gradations
rubrics_metrics.description: The West affords 'new lights and shades'—transparent lilacs and grays, rarefied atmospheres, and inimitable aerial perspectives that are essential to accurate depiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Landscape painters and colorists should study and reproduce these atmospheric hues and gradations—close-range variety and distant veilings alike—and be prepared to revise or abandon prior palettes that do not reflect these effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke elemental, grand emotions rather than merely classical form
rubrics_metrics.description: The American landscape 'awakes those grandest and subtlest element-emotions in the human soul' that marble temples, sculptures, and conventional European art probably cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to elicit deep, elemental feeling and an untrammelled sense of nature's power in readers/viewers; prioritize emotional and sensory impact over strict adherence to inherited classical forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fresh local vocabulary and precise particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Common terms like 'far, large, vast' are insufficient for writing about the Plains; new words and close particulars (cactuses, buffalo grass, dry rivers, dug-outs, cow-boys) are needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ specific regional details and invent or choose language that conveys the singular scale, textures, and phenomena of the West to achieve authenticity and avoid clichés.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select subjects with enduring esthetic resonance (prairies as lasting motifs)
rubrics_metrics.description: While some natural shows stun briefly, the Prairies and Plains 'last longer, fill the esthetic sense fuller, precede all the rest, and make North America's characteristic landscape.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor subjects that yield sustained aesthetic returns—landscapes and themes that endure in memory and can sustain a native artistic tradition, rather than transient spectacles alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate modernity and human industry into landscape representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs of man's 'restless advent'—railroads, telegraphs, steam saw-mills, smelting works—appear throughout the region and are part of the contemporary scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict the coexistence and tension between primitive Nature and modern technology; include telegraphs, railways, camps, and industrial scenes as authentic elements of Western life rather than treating the landscape as untouched wilderness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt form and diction to democratic audiences (oratory and prose fit the occasion)
rubrics_metrics.description: New American oratory (exemplified by President Hayes's impromptu addresses) is 'face-to-face,' topical, and adapted to democratic occasions rather than classical rules of dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing popular audiences, favor plain, direct, timely speech and an intimate manner over ornate, classical rhetoric; let purpose and audience determine tone and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject slavish imitation of foreign literary models
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevailing British and imported poets are 'foreign to our States' and often 'cramp'd' or anachronistic for American purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not simply reproduce British models; rather, study American materials and modes of life and develop native idioms and standards that reflect the country's conditions and characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance technical virtuosity with moral and affective warmth
rubrics_metrics.description: On Edgar Poe: 'electric lights of imaginative literature, brilliant and dazzling, but with no heat'—technical brilliance without moral principle or human warmth is incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for technical mastery (form, rhyme, craft) while ensuring the work carries substantive moral feeling or human heat so it affects readers beyond surface dazzle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow national material conditions to shape literary development
rubrics_metrics.description: Whitman argues that building a great national literature follows material foundations—prosperity, intercommunication, freedom, and mass vitality—being established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that social and economic contexts influence what literature can emerge and be received; consider how infrastructural and democratic realities (railroads, commerce, popular vitality) enable certain literary voices and themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and render human types and regional character
rubrics_metrics.description: The West supplies distinctive human figures—miners, cow-boys, packers, settlers—whose physiognomy, habits, and social roles are essential local material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray regional character honestly and use local human types to root narratives and poems in social reality; their presence helps constitute an authentic national literature.
